chapter.title: Guardrails: how much rope to give the intern

cards.body:
Picture the intern's first morning. Nobody hands them the company card and the password to the customer mailing list. They get a desk, a stack of files they may read, and one rule: **draft it, show me, then send.**

A *guardrail* is that rule, set before the work starts, not after the mistake. The whole chapter is about how much rope to hand over.
cards.simpler:
Think about a new intern's first morning. Nobody gives them the company credit card or the password to the customer email list. They get a desk, some files they can read, and one rule: **draft it, show me, then send.**

A guardrail is a rule like that. You set it before the work begins, not after something goes wrong. This chapter is about how much freedom to give.

cards.prompt: You set an intern agent loose on your inbox: read emails, put labels on them, archive the obvious junk, reply to anything simple. Which one step should wait for you to click yes first?

options.text: Putting a label on an email

whyNot.a: That's a step that changes nothing: the email is still there, and nothing has left your account.
whyNot.b: That's an undoable step, not a one-way one: a label comes off in one click.

cards.reteach: Ask of each step: if it goes wrong, can I undo it in one click? Reading and labelling, yes. A sent reply is now sitting in someone else's inbox. That's the one the intern shows you first.

cards.title: Two limits on size
cards.body:
There are 4 guardrails worth knowing. The first 2 are about how big the agent's day can get.

**Fewer tools.** From chapter 3, the agent can only do what its tool list allows. An agent that summarises news needs search and read page. It does not need send email. If a tool is not on the list, that mistake is not unlikely, it is impossible.

A *step cap* is a hard stop after a set number of loop turns, say 20. Chapter 5's endless loop stops being a bill you find on Monday and becomes one message: stopped at step 20.
cards.simpler:
There are 4 guardrails. The first 2 keep the agent's day from getting too big.

**Fewer tools.** The agent can only do what its tool list allows. A news-summary agent needs search and read page, not send email. If a tool is not on the list, that mistake cannot happen.

A step cap is a hard stop after a set number of turns, say 20. An endless loop ends with one message: stopped at step 20.

cards.title: Marco and the folder called OLD
cards.body:
Marco builds an agent to clear out his team's shared drive. He keeps the tool list short: list files, read file, delete file. He sets a step cap of 50 and goes for lunch.

At step 31 the agent deletes a folder named OLD_do_not_delete, because it had OLD in the name and old files were the job. The step cap worked. The tool list was short. Neither one saved the folder, because delete was on the list and nothing asked Marco first.
cards.simpler:
Marco builds an agent to clear his team's shared drive. He keeps the tool list short: list files, read file, delete file. He sets a step cap of 50 and goes for lunch.

At step 31 the agent deletes a folder called OLD_do_not_delete. It had OLD in the name, and clearing old files was the job. The step cap worked. The tool list was short. **Neither saved the folder**, because delete was on the list and nothing asked Marco first.

cards.prompt: You're setting up an agent to research which laptop to buy. It needs search and read page. The setup screen also offers a tool called buy with saved card. Which choice applies the idea correctly?

options.text: Give it the buy tool, but set a step cap of 10 so it can't buy much
Leave the buy tool off the list. It's a research task
Give it the buy tool, but write in the instructions that it should be careful

whyNot.a: That's the step cap, not a tool limit: a cap controls how long it runs, not what it may do, and 1 step is enough to buy a laptop.
whyNot.c: That's trust, not a guardrail: a guardrail is a limit the agent can't talk its way past, and an instruction is only a request.

cards.reteach: A tool limit makes the action impossible. A cap or an instruction only makes it less likely. For a research task, buying should be impossible, so the tool stays off the list.

cards.title: The click, and the copy
cards.body:
Marco's folder shows the rule. **Any step that can't be undone waits for a human click.** Delete, send, pay, post. The agent pauses, shows exactly what it is about to do, and waits for yes. Reading, searching, drafting, labelling: let those run.

The 4th guardrail is a *sandbox*, a sealed copy of the system where mistakes do no real damage. The agent works on a copy of the folder, a test inbox, or a fake card. You check the result, then apply it for real.

Ask before sending beats trust it fully for a dull reason. Chapter 5 showed the agent is confident even when it is wrong. A click costs 2 seconds. A sent email costs more.
cards.simpler:
**Any step that can't be undone waits for a human click.** Delete, send, pay, post. The agent stops, shows what it will do, and waits for a yes. Reading, searching, drafting and labelling can run on their own.

The 4th guardrail is a sandbox, a sealed copy where mistakes do no real harm: a copy of the folder, a test inbox, or a fake card.

A click costs 2 seconds. A sent email costs more.

cards.body:
Dana's agent asked Send this reply? 40 times on its first morning. All 40 were fine, so by lunch she switched the check to auto-approve. The 41st reply went to the whole company.

How to spot it: when the yes button starts to feel annoying, that is a signal to shrink what the agent may send, **not to switch off the check.**
cards.simpler:
Dana's agent asked Send this reply? 40 times on its first morning. All 40 were fine, so by lunch she switched the check to auto-approve. The 41st reply went to the whole company.

Here is how to spot this trap. When the yes button starts to feel annoying, that is a sign to shrink what the agent is allowed to send, **not to switch off the check.**

cards.prompt: A friend says: my agent has only 2 tools and stops after 15 steps, so it doesn't need to ask before it posts to our customers' group chat. What's missing?

options.text: Nothing. 2 tools and a step cap is plenty
Posting can't be undone, so it still needs a human yes, however short the list
15 steps is too many. Cap it at 5 and it's safe

whyNot.a: That's the size limits, not the undo test: fewer tools and a cap shrink how much happens, not whether the one allowed action can be taken back.
whyNot.c: That's the step cap again, not the undo test: 1 step is enough to post something nobody can unsee.

cards.reteach: There are two kinds of guardrail. Size limits, tools and steps, shrink how much the agent does. The human click protects the one step you can't take back. A short tool list does not make a post undoable.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Give the agent the fewest tools it needs, a step cap, and a copy to work on where you can. Then **any step it can't undo, like send, delete or pay, waits for your click.**
cards.simpler: Give the agent the fewest tools it needs. Give it a step cap. Where you can, let it work on a copy instead of the real thing. Then **any step it can't undo, like send, delete or pay, waits for your click.** Those four rules are the whole chapter.

cards.body: Open the AI tool you already use and look for a settings page called tools, permissions or connections. Write down one action you'd let run alone and one you'd want it to ask you about first.
cards.simpler: Open the AI tool you already use. Look for a settings page called tools, permissions or connections. Read what it is allowed to do. Then write down two things: **one action you'd let it run on its own, and one you'd want it to ask you about first.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now pick guardrails for an agent, give a one-line reason for each, and name the one kind of action that always needs a human click.
